# Summary of Alfred North Whitehead
Alfred North Whitehead (1861–1947) was a British mathematician and philosopher notable for his work in mathematics, logic, metaphysics, and education. Born in Kent, England, he excelled in mathematics at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he studied under Edward Routh and graduated as fourth wrangler. He co-authored the landmark work *Principia Mathematica* (1910–1913) with Bertrand Russell, a foundational text in 20th-century mathematical logic. Whitehead also authored *A Treatise on Universal Algebra* (1898) and *An Introduction to Mathematics* (1911), the latter aimed at a broader audience.
Whitehead’s philosophical career flourished later in life, especially after moving to Harvard University in 1924. There he developed process philosophy, emphasizing a universe of interrelated events and rejecting traditional materialist notions of fixed substances. His metaphysics highlights the primacy of relations, creativity, and experience in all entities, including inanimate matter—a stance termed panexperientialism. His major philosophical works include *Science and the Modern World* (1925) and *Process and Reality* (1929). Whitehead also made significant contributions to philosophy of education, advocating against teaching disconnected "inert ideas" and emphasizing imagination’s role in learning.
Whitehead's influence extended to theology through process theology, ecological ethics, business philosophy, and political thought. Despite the complexity and difficulty of his writings, his work has inspired diverse fields, from physics and biology to education and theology, with renewed interest globally, notably in China. His legacy is maintained through ongoing critical editions of his writings and dedicated research projects.
